title: Lamentations 1:12–22
context: Zion now speaks in her own voice, appealing to those who pass by to look and see if there is any sorrow like the sorrow with which the LORD has afflicted her in the day of his fierce anger. She tells of fire, a net, a yoke of transgressions, mighty men crushed, and a comforter far away; her children are desolate. At 1:17 the narrator’s voice returns briefly, in the third person: Zion spreads out her hands, and there is no one to comfort her. Then Zion’s speech resumes with a confession—“The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against his commandment”—and with a plea that the LORD would look on her distress, and that the enemies who are glad at her trouble would themselves be brought to the day already proclaimed. Confession, wrath, and grief are shared ground in this unit, not a new soteriological contrast. The hunger, the fallen young people, and the language of distress should be read with pastoral care and without sensational detail. 2 Kings 25, Jeremiah 39 and 52, and Deuteronomy 28 may again be named by reference without harmonizing.

verses.text: “Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look, and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which is brought on me, with which the LORD has afflicted me in the day of his fierce anger.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zion asks, “Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look, and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which is brought on me, with which the LORD has afflicted me in the day of his fierce anger.” The voice is now hers, first person, appealing for a look from those who pass. The sorrow is the LORD’s afflicting, in the day of his fierce anger. That pairing of grief and wrath is the verse’s own, and it is shared ground.

Arminian readers hear a genuine appeal to witnesses, and a real ascription of the sorrow to the LORD’s fierce anger, without treating the lament as a denial of his justice, which she will confess in verse 18.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same appeal and the same ascription: the LORD has afflicted her in the day of his fierce anger, and passers-by are asked to look at that sorrow.

Shared ground: Zion speaks, and she names both sorrow and the LORD’s anger. The traditions need not divide over the right to lament in that way.

verses.text: “From on high has he sent fire into my bones, and it prevails against them. He has spread a net for my feet. He has turned me back. He has made me desolate and I faint all day long.
verses.arminianNotes:
From on high, she says, fire has been sent into her bones, a net spread for her feet; she has been turned back, made desolate, and she faints all day long. The images are of a body and a path under judgment, and they are left as her modest, terrible report, not expanded into a medical or graphic scene.

Arminian readers hear Zion describing what she has suffered as from on high, a desolation that lasts all day, which she is allowed to tell in the first person.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same fire, net, turning back, and fainting as Zion’s account of the LORD’s afflicting already named in verse 12.

Shared ground: the speech is hers, and the desolation is real. There is no party contrast over these images.

verses.text: “The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand. They are knit together. They have come up on my neck. He made my strength fail. The Lord has delivered me into their hands, against whom I am not able to stand.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand.” The transgressions are hers; the binding is by his hand; they have come up on her neck, her strength has failed, and the Lord has delivered her into hands she cannot stand against. The yoke is the plain burden of her own transgressions, now bound upon her, not a symbol to be pressed beyond that. The verse uses “Lord” and that wording should simply be followed.

Arminian readers hear Zion accept the transgressions as her own, even while she tells how that yoke has broken her strength, a confession already underway before verse 18 names it outright.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same yoke as bound by his hand, the Lord delivering her into hands she cannot resist, with the transgressions named as hers.

Shared ground: guilt and delivery belong together here. The yoke stays a plain image of a burden she cannot throw off.

verses.text: “The Lord has set at nothing all my mighty men within me. He has called a solemn assembly against me to crush my young men. The Lord has trodden the virgin daughter of Judah as in a wine press.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord, she says, has set at nothing all her mighty men, has called a solemn assembly against her to crush her young men, and has trodden the virgin daughter of Judah as in a wine press. The “solemn assembly” is turned to a gathering for crushing; the wine press is an image of that crushing. “virgin daughter of Judah” is a title for the people, and is left as such, without comment that would sensationalize it. The fallen young men are to be named soberly.

Arminian readers hear a people crushed as in a press, her fighters set at nothing, a grief Zion is right to speak, not a victory hymn to be hurried into.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same setting-at-nothing, the assembly called to crush, and the treading in the press as Zion’s account of the Lord’s work against her young men and against Judah.

Shared ground: the verse is lament over a crushing. The traditions share the grief and the ascription.

verses.text: “For these things I weep. My eye, my eye runs down with water, because the comforter who should refresh my soul is far from me. My children are desolate, because the enemy has prevailed.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For these things I weep. My eye, my eye runs down with water, because the comforter who should refresh my soul is far from me. My children are desolate, because the enemy has prevailed.” The weeping is for what has just been told. The comforter is far; the children are desolate; the enemy has prevailed. The line about the children is left as brief and sober as the verse itself.

Arminian readers hear Zion’s tears as real, and the desolation of her children as a wound the lament is willing to name without using it as a device.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same doubled “My eye,” the far comforter, and the desolate children, with the enemy prevailing, as the close of this stretch of her speech before the narrator returns.

Shared ground: she weeps, and the children are desolate. The verse is left as it stands, without added detail.

verses.text: Zion spreads out her hands. There is no one to comfort her. The LORD has commanded concerning Jacob, that those who are around him should be his adversaries. Jerusalem is among them as an unclean thing.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Zion spreads out her hands. There is no one to comfort her.” The voice shifts back to the narrator for this verse: Zion is spoken of in the third person, still without a comforter. The LORD has commanded concerning Jacob that those around him should be his adversaries, and Jerusalem is among them as an unclean thing. The shift should be named, not smoothed away.

Arminian readers hear the narrator confirm what Zion has said: no comforter, and adversaries close around Jacob by the LORD’s command, a hard word that still belongs to the lament rather than to a new argument about standing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same third-person report as a brief return of the narrator, with the LORD’s command making neighbors into adversaries, and Jerusalem as an unclean thing among them.

Shared ground: there is still no one to comfort her. The change of voice is part of the unit’s shape, and not a theological fork.

verses.text: “The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against his commandment. Please hear all you peoples, and see my sorrow. My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zion says, “The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against his commandment.” Then she asks the peoples to hear and to see her sorrow; her young women and young men have gone into captivity. Confession and grief stand in one breath: he is righteous; she has rebelled; the young have been taken. That is shared ground, not a cue to restage a debate about a believer’s standing after a fall.

Arminian readers take the confession as genuine: the LORD is righteous, and she has rebelled, a truth she speaks while still asking others to see her sorrow, not a confession that cancels the lament.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same pairing: the LORD’s righteousness, her rebellion against his commandment, and the sorrow of young people gone into captivity.

Shared ground: confession belongs inside the lament. The verse is not turned into a soteriological contrast the passage does not require.

verses.text: “I called for my lovers, but they deceived me. My priests and my elders gave up the spirit in the city, while they sought food for themselves to refresh their souls.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I called for my lovers, but they deceived me.” Her priests and her elders gave up the spirit in the city, “while they sought food for themselves to refresh their souls.” The failed lovers, as in verse 2, are held lightly, since the verse does not name them. The death of priests and elders while seeking food is a famine-grief, and it is stated soberly and briefly, without added detail.

Arminian readers hear a call that found only deceit, and a hunger so hard that priests and elders died seeking food, a report the lament is right to make and which is not enlarged here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same deceived call and the same death of priests and elders in the city, while they sought food, as Zion’s account of failed help and famine.

Shared ground: the helpers failed, and hunger is in the city. Pastoral restraint is required here.

verses.text: “Look, LORD; for I am in distress. My heart is troubled. My heart turns over within me, for I have grievously rebelled. Abroad, the sword bereaves. At home, it is like death.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Look, LORD; for I am in distress. My heart is troubled. My heart turns over within me, for I have grievously rebelled.” Abroad, the sword bereaves; at home, it is like death. The plea to look is joined again to a confession of grievous rebellion, and to a report of sword and death. The inward language of a troubled, turning heart should be heard as grief, not examined as a spectacle.

Arminian readers hear a real prayer in distress, with rebellion named by Zion herself, and with violence abroad and a death-like state at home, all held together in one appeal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “Look, LORD,” the troubled heart, the confession of grievous rebellion, and the sword abroad and death at home, as Zion’s prayer in the aftermath of the fall.

Shared ground: she asks the LORD to look, and she does not deny her rebellion. Wrath and confession remain together.

verses.text: “They have heard that I sigh. There is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my trouble. They are glad that you have done it. You will bring the day that you have proclaimed, and they will be like me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They have heard that I sigh. There is no one to comfort me.” Her enemies have heard of her trouble and are glad that the LORD has done it. She then says, “You will bring the day that you have proclaimed, and they will be like me.” The enemies’ gladness is part of her grief; she looks to a day already proclaimed, when they will share her state. That hope is still a lament’s plea, not a finished timetable.

Arminian readers hear both the isolation and the request that the proclaimed day would meet the enemies who rejoice, a prayer the afflicted city is allowed to make.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same uncomforted sighing, the enemies’ gladness at what the LORD has done, and the word that he will bring the day he has proclaimed.

Shared ground: there is still no comforter, and a proclaimed day is left in the LORD’s hands. The verse need not be turned into a new contrast.

verses.text: “Let all their wickedness come before you. Do to them as you have done to me for all my transgressions. For my sighs are many, and my heart is faint.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Let all their wickedness come before you. Do to them as you have done to me for all my transgressions. For my sighs are many, and my heart is faint.” She asks that their wickedness be seen, and that they receive as she has received for her transgressions. She does not un-say her own guilt. The unit ends with many sighs and a faint heart, and is left there, as grief, not as a system.

Arminian readers take the imprecation as a real prayer of the wounded city, which still confesses “my transgressions” and which ends faint, not triumphant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same request that their wickedness come before the LORD, the same measure “as you have done to me” and the close in many sighs and a faint heart.

Shared ground: she asks for judgment on the enemies without denying her own transgressions. The chapter ends in faintness, and both traditions can stay with that.
